images.caption: Figure 3:Critical Role of Anchor Heads in Semantic Consistency.Masking the top 20%Anchor Headsleads to a sharp drop in subject/background consistency and a clear rise in imaging-quality drift (left), together with visible appearance drifteven within the 5-second training horizon(right). Masking the same number ofWorking Headsat random yields metrics on par with the unmasked baseline and no observable drift.

Figure 4:Anchor-head positions are input invariant.(a) Each row plots a single prompt’s per-head initial-frame attention score. The same vertical stripes are coherent across all 50 rows, meaning the same subset of heads attends strongly to the initial frame regardless of prompt. (b) Each row plots the per-head cross-prompt mean attention score at one of the four diffusion timesteps. The four rows display the same vertical stripes, indicating timestep-invariance as well.

Figure 5:Disentangled context routing.(a) Sliding window attention loses early frames as the cache rolls forward. (b) Sinked sliding window retains initial frames but routes the same context to all heads. (c) During DMD, our approach routes initial-frame context exclusively to the sparseAnchor Headswhile the majorityWorking Headsattend only to the local sliding window, preserving the natural head specialization.

Figure 6:Qualitative comparison and ablation.Self-Forcing suffers from temporal drift once the inference rollout exceeds the training horizon; Frame Sink avoids temporal drift but yields low-dynamic, conservative motion.
Ours (Disen-Forcing) is both drift-free and temporally dynamic.
The bottom block isolates the contributions of our two components: context routing andℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}.

Figure A3:Per-head attention distribution for additional baselines.Same head selection and rendering asFig.2(b), applied to Causal-Forcing (sliding-window) and the two sink-based methods LongLive and Rolling-Forcing. The same anchor/working partition appears in all three distillation pipelines.

Figure A6:Qualitative anchor-head masking comparison across prompts.Each row shows one prompt rendered under three masking conditions:no mask(baseline, left block),mask random heads(control, middle block,blue), andmask anchor heads(treatment, right block,red). Each block displays three frames spanning the 5-second clip. A brief prompt description is shown below each row. Random masking preserves visual fidelity; anchor masking produces visible identity, color, and scene drift, confirming that long-range anti-drift is carried specifically by the anchor-head subset.
